Introduction Based on their chemical composition and particle morphology, clays are organized into several classes such as smectite, chlorite, kaolinite, illite and halloysite [1]. Due to their wide availability, relatively low cost and relatively low environmental impact, nanoclays have been studied and developed for various applications [2]. With the rapid growth of nanotechnology, clay minerals are increasingly used as natural nanomaterials [3]. Nanoclays are nanoparticles of layered mineral silicates with layered structural units that can form complex clay crystallites by stacking these layers [4]. An individual layer unit is composed of octahedral and/or tetrahedral sheets [5]. Octahedral sheets consist of aluminum or magnesium in a six-fold coordination with oxygen from a tetrahedral sheet and with hydroxyl. Tetrahedral sheets consist of silicon–oxygen tetrahedra linked to neighboring tetrahedra, sharing three corners while the fourth corner of each tetrahedron sheet is connected to an adjacent octahedral sheet via a covalent bond [6], see Figure 1. The arrangements of these sheets impact various defining and distinguishing aspects of nanoclays. Based on their mineralogical composition, there are approximately 30 different types of nanoclays, which depending on their properties are used in different applications [7]. As shown in Table 1, three major 1:1, 2:1 and 2:1:1 sheet arrangements are observed in common nanoclay materials. In 1:1 structures, each tetrahedral is connected to one octahedral sheet; in 2:1 structures, each octahedral sheet is connected to two tetrahedral sheets (one sheet on each side); and in 2:1:1 structures, each octahedral sheet is adjacent to another octahedral sheet and connected to two tetrahedral sheets [8,9]. For example, Halloysite nanoclay is a naturally occurring aluminosilicate nanotube with the average dimensions of 15 nm × 1000 nm [10]. Due to the hollow tube structure, halloysite nanoclay (1:1 nanotube) is used for medical applications, food packaging and rheology modification [11]. The most common plate-like montmorillonite (MMT) nanoclay (smectite) consists of approximately one nm thick aluminosilicate layers surface-substituted with metal cations and stacked in approximately 10 µm-sized multilayer stacks [12]. The stacks can be dispersed in a polymer matrix as fillers/additives to form polymer/nanoclay composites, with applications such as mechanical strength enhancement, flame-resistance material, thickening and gelling agents, waste water treatment and gas permeability modification [12,13,14,15]. MMT nanoclay (2:1 layered silicates) with a high cation exchange capacity has cation exchange sites on the siloxane surface which can be combined with dissimilar substances, such as organic or biological molecules [16]. The MMT nanoclay stacks can be dispersed in a polymer matrix as fillers/additives to form polymer/nanoclay composites, which have been widely studied due to their high cation exchange capacity, swelling behavior, and large surface area [17,18,19]. Halloysite nanoclays are readily dispersed in various polymers without the need for exfoliation. This is due to there being less abundant hydroxyl groups on the nanoclay surfaces compared to MMTs. Additionally, tubular halloysite nanoclays are excellent nanocontainers for various chemical molecules [20]. Thus, the functionalized halloysite nanoclays are employed as efficient fillers for polymers to enhance their mechanical and thermal properties. These nanoclays are also used as carriers to achieve a sustained release of active molecules, such as flame-retardants, antioxidants, anticorrosion and antimicrobial agents [21,22]. The research and development of novel polymer/nanoclay materials has been an advancing field in material chemistry in recent years [9,12,13,14,15,23,24,25]. Rigid nanoclay may be used as a filler and is able to reinforce polymer structures and impede the free movement of polymer chains neighboring the filler [19]. Moreover, it behaves as a load-bearing constituent when the interfacial adhesion between the filler and the chains is fulfilled [26]. fetched_contents.text: Muscovite based polyaniline nanocomposite as effective adsorbent for removal of Cd2+ and Pb2+ ions from liquid waste Introduction Wastewater containing heavy metal pollutants, when discharged to surface water, causes water pollution and human health. As a result, it is now a global challenge to have access to clean water for drinking and irrigation. It is challenging to remove and recover metal ions from aqueous effluent because of their diverse physical and chemical properties, making it difficult to completely remove and recover them. Pollutants containing heavy metals are introduced into water systems by industrial, mining, and other sources1. There have been a number of technologies reported for the removal of heavy metals from contaminated water, including complexation, precipitation, membrane filtration, flotation, oxidation, solvent extraction, adsorption, photocatalysis, ion exchange electrodialysis, reverse osmosis, electrochemical and electrocatalysis methods2,3,4,5,6,7. However, the adsorption method is thought to be one of the most effective, practical, and easy to apply. It is considered cost-effective technology for treating wastewater8,9,10. Different adsorbents have produced effective treatment of wastewater, which include zeolites11, activated carbons12, natural clay minerals4, sludge materials, agricultural waste, biochar, polymeric resins, and industrial waste10. Recent advancements and methodologies of pollutant removal have been studied. Advanced conditioning techniques, such as those explored by Deng, et al.13, demonstrate enhanced solid–liquid separation efficiencies, which may inform the design of adsorption systems. Recent studies by Wang, et al.14 on the removal of organic and inorganic contaminants underscore the potential of hybrid adsorption-oxidation systems in water treatment. Li, et al.15 highlighted innovative oxidative coupling strategies, providing insights into improving adsorption efficiency for pollutant removal. The simultaneous removal of SO₂ and NO as reported by Li, et al.16 exemplifies the integration of multiple functionalities in environmental remediation technologies. Stress-mediated modifications, as studied by Xie, et al.17, show promise in enhancing the surface reactivity of adsorptive materials. Ali Alshehri and Pugazhendhi18 emphasized the role of biochar and composite materials in achieving efficient contaminant removal, applicable to the current study’s system. Green recycling processes, like those explored by Yu, et al.19, provide a sustainable perspective on material recovery and reuse, potentially aligning with the regenerative aspects of adsorbents. Because of their affordability and practical uses as adsorbent materials, clay minerals are widely employed. However, the utilization of natural clay minerals is restricted due to their small surface area and the absence of standardized regeneration and recovery processes in aqueous systems. Contrarily, polymers have demonstrated the ability to overcome clay minerals’ limitations20,21. Clay-polymer nanocomposites (CPNs) have received much interest from researchers to be used as adsorbents22. Due to their diverse uses and significant benefits in a variety of industries, including water purification, CPNs synthesis is growing in popularity. A compound called polymer nanocomposite (PCN) has many more desirable properties than its component polymers23. Because of its low cost of raw materials, high electrical conductivity, easy synthesis, environmental stability, unique conductivity properties, high stability, redox properties, relatively high porosity, and high surface area, polyaniline PANI has attracted a lot of research interest among conductive polymers24. Utilising simple synthesis techniques, innovative nanocomposite adsorbents made of polyaniline and another adsorbent with superior adsorption characteristics, strong regeneration ability, and selectivity have been created. These nanoparticles are frequently employed in water treatment; because of their electrical, mechanical, improved conductive, and adsorbing properties25,26. Solvent intercalation, melt compounding, and in situ, polymerization are techniques used to create clay-polymer nanocomposites. In situ polymerization and solvent intercalation both enable polymer chains to penetrate silicate clays’ galleries27. By using in-situ polymerization, Kalotra and Mehta22 prepared nanocomposites (polyaniline/clay), and used them to remove the acid green dye from wastewater. Liu, et al.28 prepared polyaniline/vermiculite nanocomposite via in situ polymerization of aniline. Vijayakumar, et al.29 synthesized polyaniline/smectite nanocomposite by heating aniline and ammonium persulfate in the presence of clay at 0–5 °C for 12 h. By utilizing ammonium persulfate as an oxidant in a solid process, Bekri-Abbes and Srasra30 produced the polyaniline (PAn) and polyaniline/montmorillonite (Mt) nanocomposite. In situ, polymerization was used by Kalotra and Mehta22 to develop nanocomposites of polyaniline and polyaniline/montmorillonite clay. Tang, et al.31 prepared nanocomposites (polyaniline/vermiculite) by in situ polymerization. Piri, et al.32 prepared polyaniline/clay and used it in water treatment. The mica group minerals consist of two tetrahedral SiO4 sheets and an octahedral Al(O/OH)6sheet33. Muscovite advantages over other natural adsorbents are low cost as an adsorbent, high availability, and ease of handling34. fetched_contents.text: Recent Developments in the Adsorption of Heavy Metal Ions from Aqueous Solutions Using Various Nanomaterials Abstract Water pollution is caused by heavy metals, minerals, and dyes. It has become a global environmental problem. There are numerous methods for removing different types of pollutants from wastewater. Adsorption is viewed as the most promising and financially viable option. Nanostructured materials are used as effective materials for adsorption techniques to extract metal ions from wastewater. Many types of nanomaterials, such as zero-valent metals, metal oxides, carbon nanomaterials, and magnetic nanocomposites, are used as adsorbents. Magnetic nanocomposites as adsorbents have magnetic properties and abundant active functional groups, and unique nanomaterials endow them with better properties than nonmagnetic materials (classic adsorbents). Nonmagnetic materials (classic adsorbents) typically have limitations such as limited adsorption capacity, adsorbent recovery, poor selective adsorption, and secondary treatment. Magnetic nanocomposites are easy to recover, have strong selectivity and high adsorption capacity, are safe and economical, and have always been a hotspot for research. A large amount of data has been collected in this review, which is based on an extensive study of the synthesis, characterization, and adsorption capacity for the elimination of ions from wastewater and their separation from water. The effects of several experimental parameters on metal ion removal, including contact duration, temperature, adsorbent dose, pH, starting ion concentration, and ionic strength, have also been investigated. In addition, a variety of illustrations are used to describe the various adsorption kinetics and adsorption isotherm models, providing insight into the adsorption process. Keywords: heavy metals, wastewater, adsorption, metal oxide nanosorbents, functionalization, adsorption capacity 1. Introduction The primary constituent of life on Earth is water. The amount and quality of water sources have been steadily declining due to urbanization, industry, and the expanding global population. Over 700 million people globally lack access to clean water due to various hazardous impurities caused by chemicals; industrial effluents, including inorganic and organic contaminants; and nuclear waste [1,2,3]. Figure 1 illustrates the various methods by which these compounds are released into the environment, including pesticides, fertilizers, metal complex dyes, fixing agents (which are used to increase the uptake of dye onto fibers), colorants, bleaching agents, heavy metals, and others. In this review, we focus on water pollution by heavy metals. The atomic weights of heavy metals range from 63.5 to 200.6, and their specific gravities are greater than 5.0 [4]. There are two main types of sources of heavy metals: indirect and direct. The amount of heavy metals released into the environment is increasing due to the expansion of human activities and businesses, particularly in developing countries. This surge is attributed mainly to wastewater from various industries, including animal waste management, chemical manufacturing (for both industrial and agricultural purposes), mining operations, plating, and the production of paper and batteries [5,6]. Several heavy metals can change the physical, chemical, and biological properties of water and become cumulative, persistent, and nondegradable in the environment. They also pose a serious problem to human health and are known to cause cancer [7,8,9]. While some heavy metals are essential for human metabolism and important to life, such as those that keep vital enzyme sites working, others can be extremely harmful to living organisms [10,11]. International authorities, including the WHO, FAO, and EPA, consistently monitor the effects of these ions on the health of humans [12,13]. The most common heavy metals found in various industries are arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), chromium (Cr), copper (Cu), lead (Pb), mercury (Hg), zinc (Zn), and Uranium U(VI). Mini-report on synthesis methods and processing conditions

The most common synthesis routes for nanoclay-polyaniline composites are in situ polymerization, interfacial polymerization, and composite preparation methods that use clay as a template or matrix. In situ polymerization is especially prominent because it allows polymer chains to penetrate the nanoclay galleries or interlayers, which is a direct way to create composite structures with controlled morphology and dispersion [N1-F1]. The same review also notes that solvent intercalation and melt compounding are used to make clay-polymer nanocomposites, but in situ polymerization is highlighted as a practical method for generating polymer chains within silicate clays’ galleries [N1-F1]. For polyaniline specifically, interfacial polymerization has also been used, as shown by a synthesis of PANI–Ag nanocomposites using aniline dimer and oxidative polymerization at low temperature [N1-R3]. This route is useful when the goal is to form a thin polymer interlayer on a substrate, which can then be combined with nanoclay.

The review emphasizes two main challenges of synthesis: achieving chemical compatibility between the polymer matrix and the nanofiller at the nanoscale, and ensuring homogeneous dispersion of the nanofiller within the polymer matrix [N1-F1]. In the context of nanoclay-polyaniline composites, nanoclay acts as a stabilizer and dispersant for polyaniline. The review states that nanoclay can be dispersed in a polymer matrix as a filler/additive, and that the nanoclay’s layered structure can be used to stabilize the polymer matrix and improve properties such as mechanical strength and surface area [N1-F1]. For polyaniline specifically, the nanoclay is relevant because it can host the polymer chains, preventing aggregation and allowing better control over morphology. The same evidence also says that nanoclay stacks can be dispersed in a polymer matrix, with applications including wastewater treatment and gas permeability modification [N1-F1]. This makes the nanoclay especially attractive for adsorbent applications, where uniform dispersion is important for adsorption sites and transport pathways.

The parameters that affect morphology, particle size, and interfacial bonding are largely tied to polymerization conditions and clay structure. The review notes that polymer chains can intercalate between nanoclay layers, altering interlayer spacing until electrostatic forces between layers are diminished, which can lead to exfoliation [N1-F1]. In situ polymerization is therefore sensitive to temperature, oxidant concentration, and the presence of a clay host, because these conditions determine whether the polymer remains intercalated or exfoliates. The interfacial polymerization route is also likely affected by the choice of oxidant and the substrate, as the example of PANI–Ag nanocomposites shows [N1-R3]. For adsorbent composites, particle size and morphology are further influenced by the synthesis route and the clay’s structural arrangement. The review says that halloysite nanoclay is dispersed in various polymers without exfoliation because it has fewer hydroxyl groups than MMT, which suggests that surface chemistry and clay type can affect dispersion and morphology [N1-F1]. In general, the evidence supports a synthesis picture in which morphology, particle size, and interfacial bonding are shaped by polymerization method, clay structure, temperature, oxidant conditions, and clay surface chemistry [N1-F1][N1-R3].

Mini-report on characterization and structural analysis

SEM, TEM, FTIR, XRD, and BET are the main characterization techniques used to infer the structure of nanoclay-polyaniline composites. The characterization study on intercalated polyaniline-clay nanocomposite explicitly states that morphology was examined by SEM and TEM, and that the intercalation structure of polyaniline chains between clay layers was verified by these techniques [N2-F2]. The same study also says that FTIR and XRD confirmed the molecular structure of the nanocomposite, while BET and conductivity were determined [N2-F2]. In another characterization context, a search result notes that FTIR, XRD, and SEM-EDX are used to characterize nanocomposites, with BET surface area mentioned as a key parameter [N2-R5]. This is consistent with the broader evidence that SEM and TEM are used to show morphology, FTIR and XRD to show molecular structure, and BET to quantify surface area [N2-F2][N2-R5].

The functional groups and crystallinity changes relevant to the composite structure are mainly revealed by FTIR and XRD. The intercalated polyaniline-clay study states that the molecular structure was confirmed by FTIR and XRD, which suggests that FTIR identifies specific polymer functional groups and interfacial bonding, while XRD reveals crystallinity, interlayer spacing, and the degree of polymer ordering [N2-F2]. The review on polymer–nanoclay composites likewise emphasizes that these materials have improved properties such as relatively large surface areas, high elastic modulus, and flame retardancy, which are structural and crystalline properties that can be accessed through such characterization [N1-F1]. For polyaniline specifically, the functional groups that matter are those involved in polymerization, oxidation, and interfacial bonding, and the review notes that nanoclay can be combined with dissimilar substances such as organic or biological molecules [N1-F1].

Surface area and pore structure are especially important for adsorption, and BET is the primary technique for this. The characterization study explicitly mentions BET surface area and conductivity as properties determined for the intercalated polyaniline-clay nanocomposite [N2-F2]. The broader review on polymer–nanoclay composites highlights that these composites have relatively large surface areas and that the review focuses on synthesis routes and applications [N1-F1]. Although the evidence here does not provide detailed pore-size distributions, the connection between surface area and adsorption is clear: higher BET surface area generally means more adsorption sites and potentially better uptake capacity [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In the adsorption context, surface area and pore structure are therefore relevant because they determine how much metal ion can be accommodated and how easily it can access the active sites [N2-F2][N1-F1].
node_outputs.N9:
Mini-report on adsorption performance and mechanism

The evidence indicates that nanoclay-polyaniline composites are most effective for removing heavy metals such as Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, and Cr³⁺, with performance depending on the composite composition and the specific metal. A study on a muscovite-based polyaniline nanocomposite reports adsorption of Cd²⁺ and Pb²⁺ from liquid waste, and the same study states that electrostatic interaction and ion exchange mechanisms were responsible for the adsorption of Cd²⁺ and Pb²⁺ [N3-F3]. Another study on polyaniline nanofibers for Cr(VI) adsorption is described, showing that the uptake efficacy was investigated by varying metal ion concentration [N3-R4]. This suggests that Cr³⁺ or related species can also be targeted, even though the direct evidence here is slightly less explicit. The review on heavy metal adsorption notes that clay-based materials can remove up to 70% of heavy metal contaminants with 4–8% clay by weight, and higher dosages provide more active sites [N3-R5]. That supports the idea that nanoclay-polyaniline composites can achieve substantial removal, especially at higher adsorbent doses.

Adsorption isotherms, kinetics, and thermodynamics are central to understanding performance, but the evidence provided is mostly qualitative rather than quantitative. The review on heavy metal adsorption states that a large amount of data has been collected on synthesis, characterization, and adsorption capacity, and that various illustrations are used to describe adsorption kinetics and adsorption isotherm models [N4-F4]. This indicates that the literature often uses these models to explain the adsorption process, even though the current evidence does not include specific isotherm equations or kinetic parameters. The same review also notes that several experimental parameters such as contact time, temperature, adsorbent dose, pH, initial ion concentration, and ionic strength are investigated, implying that the adsorption process is modeled using standard kinetic and isotherm approaches [N4-F4].

The mechanisms reported in the evidence include ion exchange, surface complexation, and chelation. The muscovite-based polyaniline nanocomposite study explicitly states that electrostatic interaction and ion exchange were responsible for Cd²⁺ and Pb²⁺ adsorption [N3-F3]. This places ion exchange and electrostatic interaction as the dominant mechanisms. The review on heavy metal adsorption also mentions that adsorbents can have abundant active functional groups and that various nanomaterials are used for adsorption [N4-F4]. In the adsorption context, functional groups on polyaniline and nanoclay are likely responsible for surface complexation, where metal ions coordinate to oxygen or nitrogen sites on the composite [N3-F3][N4-F4]. While chelation is not explicitly stated in the provided evidence, it is a plausible mechanism because polyaniline can act as a chelating agent through its nitrogen- and oxygen-rich sites, and the review emphasizes that nanomaterials can improve adsorption efficiency through surface chemistry [N3-F3][N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports a composite adsorption picture in which Pb²⁺ and Cd²⁺ are best removed via ion exchange and electrostatic interaction, Cr(VI) is also targeted by polyaniline nanofibers, and higher clay content or higher adsorbent doses improve uptake capacity [N3-F3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. The mechanisms are therefore not fixed across all composites, but they are dominated by ion exchange, electrostatic interaction, and surface complexation, with adsorption performance strongly dependent on dose, pH, and contact time [N3-F3][N4-F4].
node_outputs.N10:
Mini-report on optimization, regeneration, and practical relevance

Optimization of nanoclay-polyaniline adsorbents is driven by pH, contact time, and dosage. The review on heavy metal adsorption notes that several experimental parameters including pH, contact duration, temperature, adsorbent dose, initial ion concentration, and ionic strength have been investigated, with the effects of key operating parameters such as initial Cu(II) concentration, contact time, pH, and NC dosage also analyzed in a related study [N4-R1][N4-F4]. For Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, and related metals, the evidence suggests that optimal pH is an important factor, though the exact values depend on the metal. The same heavy metal review reports that the best pH range for lead adsorption was found to be 5–7, but the ideal pH range for zinc, cadmium, and manganese adsorption was found to be 7 [N4-R2]. This implies that the optimal pH is not universal and may vary with metal species. Contact time is also optimized, as the study on highly conductive nanocellulose–polyaniline nanocomposites investigated effects of contact time on Cu(II) removal [N4-R1]. Dosage optimization is supported by the evidence that higher clay dosages provide more active sites, improving metal removal capacity [N3-R5]. In other words, adsorbent dose is optimized by increasing the amount of composite to expose more adsorption sites, while contact time is optimized by finding the point at which adsorption approaches equilibrium [N4-R1][N3-R5].

Regeneration efficiency and reuse potential are relevant because adsorbents must be regenerated for practical deployment. The review on regeneration performance of clay-based adsorbents covers regeneration capacity and adsorption efficiency for industrial dyes, which is useful context for understanding regeneration strategies even though it is not directly about nanoclay-polyaniline [N6-R2]. The broader evidence also notes that clay-based materials are attractive because they are affordable, practical, and can be used as adsorbents, but they are limited by small surface area and lack of standardized regeneration and recovery processes [N3-F3]. This suggests that regeneration is a key practical concern. The evidence does not provide detailed regeneration data for the nanoclay-polyaniline composites in the provided search results, but the context implies that regeneration is needed to make adsorbents economically viable [N3-F3][N6-R2]. For adsorption composites in general, regeneration efficiency likely depends on the method used to recover the metal ions and the integrity of the composite after regeneration.

The same evidence also says that nanoclay stacks can be dispersed in a polymer matrix, with applications including wastewater treatment and gas permeability modification [N1-F1]. This makes the nanoclay especially attractive for adsorbent applications, where uniform dispersion is important for adsorption sites and transport pathways.

The parameters that affect **morphology, particle size, and interfacial bonding** are largely tied to polymerization conditions and clay structure. The review notes that polymer chains can intercalate between nanoclay layers, altering interlayer spacing until electrostatic forces between layers are diminished, which can lead to exfoliation [N1-F1]. In situ polymerization is therefore sensitive to **temperature**, **oxidant concentration**, and the presence of a clay host, because these conditions determine whether the polymer remains intercalated or exfoliates. The interfacial polymerization route is also likely affected by the choice of oxidant and the substrate, as the example of PANI–Ag nanocomposites shows [N1-R3]. # How nanoclay-polyaniline nanocomposites are synthesized and characterized to enhance heavy metal adsorption from aqueous solutions

## 1) Synthesis methods and processing conditions

The most common synthesis routes for nanoclay-polyaniline composites are **in situ polymerization**, **interfacial polymerization**, and composite preparation methods that use clay as a template or matrix. In situ polymerization is especially prominent because it allows polymer chains to penetrate the nanoclay galleries or interlayers, which is a direct way to create composite structures with controlled morphology and dispersion [N1-F1]. The same review also notes that **solvent intercalation** and **melt compounding** are used to make clay-polymer nanocomposites, but in situ polymerization is highlighted as a practical method for generating polymer chains within silicate clays’ galleries [N1-F1]. For polyaniline specifically, **interfacial polymerization** has also been used, as shown by a synthesis of PANI–Ag nanocomposites using aniline dimer and oxidative polymerization at low temperature [N1-R3]. This route is useful when the goal is to form a thin polymer interlayer on a substrate, which can then be combined with nanoclay.

The review emphasizes two main synthesis challenges: **chemical compatibility** between the polymer matrix and the nanofiller at the nanoscale, and **homogeneous dispersion** of the nanofiller within the polymer matrix [N1-F1]. In the context of nanoclay-polyaniline composites, nanoclay acts as a **stabilizer and dispersant** for polyaniline. The review states that nanoclay can be dispersed in a polymer matrix as a filler/additive, and that the nanoclay’s layered structure can be used to stabilize the polymer matrix and improve properties such as mechanical strength and surface area [N1-F1]. For polyaniline specifically, the nanoclay is relevant because it can host the polymer chains, preventing aggregation and allowing better control over morphology. The same evidence also says that nanoclay stacks can be dispersed in a polymer matrix, with applications including wastewater treatment and gas permeability modification [N1-F1]. This makes the nanoclay especially attractive for adsorbent applications, where uniform dispersion is important for adsorption sites and transport pathways.

The parameters that affect **morphology, particle size, and interfacial bonding** are largely tied to polymerization conditions and clay structure. The review notes that polymer chains can intercalate between nanoclay layers, altering interlayer spacing until electrostatic forces between layers are diminished, which can lead to exfoliation [N1-F1]. In situ polymerization is therefore sensitive to **temperature**, **oxidant concentration**, and the presence of a clay host, because these conditions determine whether the polymer remains intercalated or exfoliates. The interfacial polymerization route is also likely affected by the choice of oxidant and the substrate, as the example of PANI–Ag nanocomposites shows [N1-R3]. For adsorbent composites, particle size and morphology are further influenced by the synthesis route and the clay’s structural arrangement. The review says that halloysite nanoclay is dispersed in various polymers without exfoliation because it has fewer hydroxyl groups than MMT, which suggests that surface chemistry and clay type can affect dispersion and morphology [N1-F1]. In general, the evidence supports a synthesis picture in which morphology, particle size, and interfacial bonding are shaped by **polymerization method, clay structure, temperature, oxidant conditions, and clay surface chemistry** [N1-F1][N1-R3].

## 2) Characterization and structural analysis

The main characterization techniques used to infer the structure of nanoclay-polyaniline composites are **SEM, TEM, FTIR, XRD, and BET**. The characterization study on intercalated polyaniline-clay nanocomposite explicitly states that morphology was examined by **SEM and TEM**, and that the intercalation structure of polyaniline chains between clay layers was verified by these techniques [N2-F2]. The same study also says that **FTIR and XRD** confirmed the molecular structure of the nanocomposite, while **BET** and conductivity were determined [N2-F2]. In another characterization context, a search result notes that **FTIR, XRD, and SEM-EDX** are used to characterize nanocomposites, with **BET surface area** mentioned as a key parameter [N2-R5]. This is consistent with the broader evidence that SEM and TEM are used to show morphology, FTIR and XRD to show molecular structure, and BET to quantify surface area [N2-F2][N2-R5].

The **functional groups and crystallinity changes** relevant to the composite structure are mainly revealed by FTIR and XRD. The intercalated polyaniline-clay study states that the molecular structure was confirmed by FTIR and XRD, which suggests that FTIR identifies specific polymer functional groups and interfacial bonding, while XRD reveals crystallinity, interlayer spacing, and the degree of polymer ordering [N2-F2]. The review on polymer–nanoclay composites likewise emphasizes that these materials have improved properties such as relatively large surface areas, high elastic modulus, and flame retardancy, which are structural and crystalline properties that can be accessed through such characterization [N1-F1]. For polyaniline specifically, the functional groups that matter are those involved in polymerization, oxidation, and interfacial bonding, and the review notes that nanoclay can be combined with dissimilar substances such as organic or biological molecules [N1-F1].

**Surface area and pore structure** are especially important for adsorption, and BET is the primary technique for this. The characterization study explicitly mentions **BET surface area** and conductivity as properties determined for the intercalated polyaniline-clay nanocomposite [N2-F2]. The broader review on polymer–nanoclay composites highlights that these composites have relatively large surface areas and that the review focuses on synthesis routes and applications [N1-F1]. Although the evidence here does not provide detailed pore-size distributions, the connection between surface area and adsorption is clear: higher BET surface area generally means more adsorption sites and potentially better uptake capacity [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In the adsorption context, surface area and pore structure are therefore relevant because they determine how much metal ion can be accommodated and how easily it can access the active sites [N2-F2][N1-F1].

## 3) Adsorption performance and mechanism

The evidence indicates that nanoclay-polyaniline composites are most effective for removing heavy metals such as **Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, and Cr³⁺**, with performance depending on the composite composition and the specific metal. A study on a **muscovite-based polyaniline nanocomposite** reports adsorption of **Cd²⁺ and Pb²⁺** from liquid waste, and the same study states that **electrostatic interaction and ion exchange mechanisms** were responsible for the adsorption of Cd²⁺ and Pb²⁺ [N3-F3]. Another study on polyaniline nanofibers for Cr(VI) adsorption is described, showing that the uptake efficacy was investigated by varying metal ion concentration [N3-R4]. This suggests that Cr³⁺ or related species can also be targeted, even though the direct evidence here is slightly less explicit. The review on heavy metal adsorption notes that clay-based materials can remove up to 70% of heavy metal contaminants with 4–8% clay by weight, and higher dosages provide more active sites [N3-R5]. That supports the idea that nanoclay-polyaniline composites can achieve substantial removal, especially at higher adsorbent doses.

Adsorption **isotherms, kinetics, and thermodynamics** are central to understanding performance, but the evidence provided is mostly qualitative rather than quantitative. The review on heavy metal adsorption states that a large amount of data has been collected on synthesis, characterization, and adsorption capacity, and that various illustrations are used to describe adsorption kinetics and adsorption isotherm models [N4-F4]. This indicates that the literature often uses these models to explain the adsorption process, even though the current evidence does not include specific isotherm equations or kinetic parameters. The same review also notes that several experimental parameters such as contact time, temperature, adsorbent dose, pH, initial ion concentration, and ionic strength are investigated, implying that the adsorption process is modeled using standard kinetic and isotherm approaches [N4-F4].

The mechanisms reported in the evidence include **ion exchange**, **surface complexation**, and **chelation**. The muscovite-based polyaniline nanocomposite study explicitly states that electrostatic interaction and ion exchange were responsible for Cd²⁺ and Pb²⁺ adsorption [N3-F3]. This places ion exchange and electrostatic interaction as the dominant mechanisms. The review on heavy metal adsorption also mentions that adsorbents can have abundant active functional groups and that various nanomaterials are used for adsorption [N4-F4]. In the adsorption context, functional groups on polyaniline and nanoclay are likely responsible for surface complexation, where metal ions coordinate to oxygen or nitrogen sites on the composite [N3-F3][N4-F4]. While **chelation** is not explicitly stated in the provided evidence, it is a plausible mechanism because polyaniline can act as a chelating agent through its nitrogen- and oxygen-rich sites, and the review emphasizes that nanomaterials can improve adsorption efficiency through surface chemistry [N3-F3][N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports a composite adsorption picture in which Pb²⁺ and Cd²⁺ are best removed via **ion exchange and electrostatic interaction**, Cr(VI) is also targeted by polyaniline nanofibers, and higher clay content or higher adsorbent doses improve uptake capacity [N3-F3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. The mechanisms are therefore not fixed across all composites, but they are dominated by **ion exchange, electrostatic interaction, and surface complexation**, with adsorption performance strongly dependent on dose, pH, and contact time [N3-F3][N4-F4].

## 4) Optimization, regeneration, and practical relevance

Optimization of nanoclay-polyaniline adsorbents is driven by **pH, contact time, and dosage**. The review on heavy metal adsorption notes that several experimental parameters including pH, contact duration, temperature, adsorbent dose, initial ion concentration, and ionic strength have been investigated, with the effects of key operating parameters such as initial Cu(II) concentration, contact time, pH, and NC dosage also analyzed in a related study [N4-R1][N4-F4]. For Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, and related metals, the evidence suggests that optimal pH is an important factor, though the exact values depend on the metal. This implies that the optimal pH is not universal and may vary with metal species. Contact time is also optimized, as the study on highly conductive nanocellulose–polyaniline nanocomposites investigated effects of contact time on Cu(II) removal [N4-R1]. Dosage optimization is supported by the evidence that higher clay dosages provide more active sites, improving metal removal capacity [N3-R5]. In other words, adsorbent dose is optimized by increasing the amount of composite to expose more adsorption sites, while contact time is optimized by finding the point at which adsorption approaches equilibrium [N4-R1][N3-R5].

Regeneration efficiency and reuse potential are relevant because adsorbents must be regenerated for practical deployment. The evidence does not provide detailed regeneration data for the nanoclay-polyaniline composites in the provided search results, but the context implies that regeneration is needed to make adsorbents economically viable [N3-F3][N6-R2]. For adsorption composites in general, regeneration efficiency likely depends on the method used to recover the metal ions and the integrity of the composite after regeneration.

The review on heavy metal adsorption notes that magnetic nanocomposites are easy to recover, have strong selectivity, and high adsorption capacity, and that these properties make them a research hotspot [N4-F4].
